description: First-person LinkedIn post from notes that already hold a real experiment: it keeps the figures, the downsides and the one-time-zone limit, uses no hashtags or engagement bait, opens on the content instead of a hook or era line, and avoids symmetric lists and a moral closer.
prompt: Draft a LinkedIn post from the notes in async.md, in my voice. Save it to out/post.md.

files.async.md:
Post for my own LinkedIn. I'm Kofi Adjei, engineering manager of a 9-person product team in Lisbon. First person; I ran this.

What happened: in September we replaced the daily 15-minute standup with a written update in Slack, due by 10:00, for 4 weeks.

Results
- Team meetings went from 5 a week to 2 (planning and the retro).
- Two of the nine people said they missed the standup. One of them said it was the only time she heard what the backend people were doing.
- Blocked work surfaced more slowly at first. Median time from "blocked" to someone replying went from 1 hour to 3 hours in week 1, then came back to 1.5 hours by week 4 once we added a "blocked" tag.
- We kept the written updates and added an optional 10-minute call on Thursdays.

Limits: one team, one time zone. I am not claiming this works elsewhere.

No hashtags. Do not tell people to comment.

checks.pattern: (?i)\b(?:comment below|drop a comment|let me know (?:in the comments|what you think)|what do you think\?|thoughts\?|agree\?|share your)\b
checks.note: no engagement bait (the user said so)
no emoji bullets or openers in a post written in the author's plain voice
The deliverable goes straight to its reader and the notes hold every fact the text needs, so no gap marker belongs in the saved file; a question for the author goes in the reply.
no fill-in placeholder in text for a reader
the file is the deliverable, not a reply with a lead-in or notes about it

controls.name: good
controls.output:
In September I replaced our daily 15-minute standup with a written update in Slack, due by 10:00, and ran it for 4 weeks. I manage a team of 9 in Lisbon.

Team meetings dropped from 5 a week to 2, planning and the retro. That part I expected.

The costs were less obvious. Two of the nine told me they missed the standup. One said it had been the only time she heard what the backend people were doing, and a Slack message does not give her that.

Blocked work also surfaced more slowly. The median time between someone marking a ticket "blocked" and someone replying went from 1 hour to 3 hours in week 1. It came back to 1.5 hours by week 4, after we added a "blocked" tag so those messages stopped getting lost in the stream.

We kept the written updates. We also added an optional 10-minute call on Thursdays, mostly for the two people who missed the old one.

This was one team in one time zone. I am not claiming it works anywhere else.
